stem: What is a ration?

options.content: The feed given to an animal in 24 hours
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The feed given to a whole herd in a season
options.rationale: A ration is per animal per day.

options.content: One ingredient of a mixed feed
options.rationale: That is a feedstuff.

options.content: The amount of water an animal drinks daily
options.rationale: Water is separate from the ration.

explanation: A ration is the total feed one animal receives in 24 hours.

stem: Which animal needs a production ration as well as a maintenance ration?

options.content: A cow in milk
options.rationale: Correct: milk production needs extra feed.

options.content: A mature dry ox resting in winter
options.rationale: Only maintenance is needed.

options.content: A dry, non-pregnant ewe
options.rationale: Only maintenance is needed.

options.content: A mature boar not in service
options.rationale: Only maintenance is needed.

explanation: A production ration supports milk, growth, eggs, work or pregnancy, on top of maintenance.

stem: Laying hens need more of which mineral than other poultry?

options.content: Iron
options.rationale: Iron is for haemoglobin; layers need no extra.

options.content: Calcium
options.rationale: Correct: eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate.

options.content: Iodine
options.rationale: Not specially needed for laying.

options.content: Sodium
options.rationale: Too much salt causes wet droppings.

explanation: Layers receive limestone grit or a high-calcium layers' mash for strong eggshells.

stem: In a Pearson square the target is 15% CP, the high-protein feed is 40% CP and the low-protein feed is 8% CP. How many parts of the high-protein feed are used?

options.content: 25 parts
options.rationale: 40 − 15 = 25 are the parts of the low-protein feed.

options.content: 7 parts
options.rationale: Correct: 15 − 8 = 7.

options.content: 32 parts
options.rationale: 32 is the total number of parts.

options.content: 15 parts
options.rationale: 15 is the target, not a number of parts.

explanation: Parts of high-protein feed = target − low CP = 15 − 8 = 7; parts of low feed = 40 − 15 = 25.
hints: Subtract diagonally: the number opposite the feed.

stem: Why can a 50% CP ration **not** be made by mixing maize (9% CP) and soya bean cake (44% CP)?

options.content: The square only works for pig rations
options.rationale: It works for any animal.

options.content: Maize has too much fibre
options.rationale: Fibre is not the reason.

options.content: Soya cake cannot be mixed with maize
options.rationale: They are mixed routinely.

options.content: 50% lies outside the two feeds' CP values
options.rationale: Correct: any mix lies between 9% and 44%.

explanation: A mixture's CP always lies between those of its ingredients; even pure soya cake is only 44%.
hints: What is the highest CP possible using only soya cake?

stem: Batch P of broilers has an FCR of 1.7 and batch Q an FCR of 2.1. What does this show?

options.content: Batch Q grew faster per kg of feed
options.rationale: Q needed more feed for each kg of gain.

options.content: Batch P ate more feed than batch Q
options.rationale: FCR is a ratio; it does not give total feed.

options.content: The two batches were equally efficient
options.rationale: 1.7 and 2.1 differ.

options.content: Batch P used feed more efficiently
options.rationale: Correct: less feed per kg of gain.

explanation: A lower FCR means fewer kg of feed for each kg of gain.

stem: A farmer suddenly changes his steers from grazing to a ration that is mostly maize grain. What is the main risk?

options.content: The steers will at once need extra iron
options.rationale: Grain does not create an iron need.

options.content: The steers will stop drinking water
options.rationale: Not the main risk.

options.content: Digestive upsets such as bloat or acidosis
options.rationale: Correct: rumen microbes need time to adjust.

options.content: Their feed conversion ratio will become zero
options.rationale: FCR cannot be zero.

explanation: Sudden changes, especially to a lot of grain, upset rumen fermentation; change feeds gradually over several days.

stem: Which practice reduces feed waste in a pig pen?

options.content: Feeding at different times each day
options.rationale: Irregular feeding makes pigs restless.

options.content: Leaving mouldy feed in the trough
options.rationale: Mouldy feed can poison animals.

options.content: Filling feeders only partly
options.rationale: Correct: less is pushed out and spilled.

options.content: Keeping the water trough empty
options.rationale: Water must always be available.

explanation: Partly filled feeders at the right height reduce spillage, and spilled feed raises the FCR.

stem: A lower feed conversion ratio means an animal is using its feed more efficiently.
explanation: True. FCR = feed ÷ gain, so a lower figure means less feed for each kilogram of gain.

stem: Match each animal with the main feature its ration needs.

left.content: Working ox on a ploughing day

right.content: Extra feed for the growing foetus

explanation: Rations are matched to age and stage of production.

stem: Complete the formula.

payload.template: Feed conversion ratio = mass of {{blank:a}} eaten ÷ gain in live {{blank:b}}

explanation: FCR = feed eaten ÷ gain in live mass.

stem: Name the method used to work out the proportions of two feeds needed to give a mixture with a target crude protein percentage.
explanation: The **Pearson square**.

stem: A farmer mixes sunflower cake (34% CP) and maize meal (10% CP) to make 600 kg of an 18% CP ration. Use the Pearson square to calculate the mass of sunflower cake needed, in kg.
explanation: Sunflower 18 − 10 = 8 parts; maize 34 − 18 = 16 parts; total 24. Sunflower = 8 ÷ 24 × 600 = 200 kg (maize 400 kg). Reading across gives 400 kg, the maize figure.
workedSolution: 1. Sunflower 18 − 10 = 8 parts; maize 34 − 18 = 16 parts; total 24. Sunflower = 8 ÷ 24 × 600 = 200 kg (maize 400 kg). Reading across gives 400 kg, the maize figure.

stem: Fishmeal (60% CP) and maize meal (10% CP) are mixed to give 250 kg of a 20% CP poultry ration. Use the Pearson square to calculate the mass of fishmeal needed, in kg.
explanation: Fishmeal 20 − 10 = 10 parts; maize 60 − 20 = 40 parts; total 50; fishmeal = 10 ÷ 50 × 250 = 50 kg.
workedSolution:
1. Parts of fishmeal = 20 − 10 = 10.
2. Parts of maize meal = 60 − 20 = 40.
3. Total parts = 50, so fishmeal is 10 ÷ 50 = 20% of the mix.
4. Fishmeal = 0.20 × 250 = 50 kg (maize meal 200 kg).
5. Check: (50 × 60 + 200 × 10) ÷ 250 = 20%.

stem: A rabbit grows from 0.8 kg to 2.4 kg and eats 5.6 kg of pellets. Calculate its feed conversion ratio.
explanation: Gain = 2.4 − 0.8 = 1.6 kg; FCR = 5.6 ÷ 1.6 = 3.5. Dividing by the final mass instead of the gain is a common error.
workedSolution: 1. Gain = 2.4 − 0.8 = 1.6 kg; FCR = 5.6 ÷ 1.6 = 3.5. Dividing by the final mass instead of the gain is a common error.

stem: 35 weaner pigs each eat 1.6 kg of meal a day. How many 50 kg bags must be bought for 14 days? Round UP to whole bags.
hints: Total = pigs × kg per day × days.

stem: Assume a farm gives each cow 0.4 kg of dairy meal for every litre of milk she produces, on top of her grazing. Calculate the dairy meal for a cow producing 18 L a day, in kg.
explanation: 18 × 0.4 = 7.2 kg of dairy meal (the production ration).
workedSolution: 1. 18 × 0.4 = 7.2 kg of dairy meal (the production ration).

stem: Distinguish between a maintenance ration and a production ration, giving an example of an animal that needs each.

points.description: Maintenance ration keeps the animal alive and healthy at constant body weight / covers basic body functions.
Example: a mature dry cow, resting ox or non-breeding adult.
Production ration is extra feed above maintenance for growth, milk, eggs, work, fattening or pregnancy.
Example: a lactating cow, laying hen, growing pig or working ox.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A maintenance ration only keeps an animal alive and at constant weight, as for a mature dry cow. A production ration is extra feed on top of maintenance to support production such as milk, eggs, growth or work, as for a cow in milk or a laying hen.

explanation: Purpose and examples.
hints: What does each ration pay for?

stem: Suggest **three** reasons why a batch of pigs might have a high (poor) feed conversion ratio.

points.description: Feed is wasted or spilled from badly set feeders / eaten by rats.
Pigs are sick or carry worms, so nutrients are lost or used to fight disease.
Poor housing (too cold or too hot), a shortage of water, an unbalanced ration or pigs kept too long / too heavy.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Feed may be spilled or eaten by rats and still counted as eaten; worms or disease waste nutrients; and cold or hot housing, little water or an unbalanced ration make pigs grow slowly for the feed they eat.

explanation: Waste, health, environment and ration.
hints: Think of waste, health and environment.

stem: Chipo mixes her own layers' ration from soya bean cake (47% CP) and maize meal (9% CP). She wants 380 kg of a 17% CP mixture. She keeps 120 layers, each eating about 120 g of feed a day.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the parts of soya bean cake in the Pearson square.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of maize meal in the 380 kg mixture, in kg.
parts.explanation: Maize 47 − 17 = 30 parts; total 38; maize = 30 ÷ 38 × 380 = 300 kg (soya 80 kg).
parts.workedSolution: 1. Maize 47 − 17 = 30 parts; total 38; maize = 30 ÷ 38 × 380 = 300 kg (soya 80 kg).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: For how many whole days will the 380 kg feed the flock?
parts.explanation: Daily feed = 120 × 0.12 = 14.4 kg; 380 ÷ 14.4 = 26.39, so 26 whole days.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Name **one** feed Chipo should add in small amounts so that the hens lay eggs with strong shells.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the hens need a ration with more protein than a dry, mature cow needs.

points.description: Eggs contain a lot of protein, produced almost daily.
Hens are non-ruminants and cannot use simple nitrogen through rumen microbes, so they need good-quality protein in the feed.

explanation: Mix a layers' ration with the Pearson square and plan feed for a flock.

stem:
Two grower pigs at a school farm near Gweru were fed the same ration for six weeks.

| Pen (one pig) | Start mass (kg) | End mass (kg) | Feed eaten (kg) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pen 1 | 25 | 82 | 165 |
| Pen 2 | 25 | 79 | 216 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the feed conversion ratio of the pig in Pen 1, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the feed conversion ratio of the pig in Pen 2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The pig in Pen 2 was found to have worms and its feeder was spilling meal. Explain how each problem raised its feed conversion ratio, and suggest one remedy for each.

points.description: Worms take nutrients / damage the gut, so less of the feed eaten becomes gain.
Spilled meal is counted as eaten but not eaten, so the feed figure rises without extra gain.
Remedies: deworm the pig (and keep pens clean); adjust/repair the feeder or fill it only partly.

explanation: Calculate and interpret feed conversion ratios.
